overview: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is damage to the brain from a blow, jolt or other outside force, ranging from concussions to severe injuries. This bill renews federal TBI programs run by the Department of Health and Human Services, including tracking and prevention work at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and grants to states for TBI services and legal advocacy, through fiscal year 2031. It expands the CDC's data collection to look at causes, risk factors and groups at higher risk, such as people injured on the job, and requires the CDC to post aggregated TBI data and prevention strategies online. It names the national tracking program after former Representative Bill Pascrell, Jr., adds tribal programs to state grant outreach and updates the legal definition of TBI. It also requires a report within two years on high-risk groups, such as domestic violence survivors and public safety officers, and a study of long-term effects of TBI, including links to dementia and mental health conditions. As of October 5, 2026, it had passed the Senate and was waiting for action in the House.
for: Supporters say renewing these programs keeps help flowing to people living with brain injuries and that better data on who is most at risk will make prevention and care more effective.
against: Critics say the bill extends spending authority for several more years while adding new reports and studies, without showing how well the existing programs have performed.
